videos.name: Y Combinator
videos.title: We Built a Company Agent and Tried To Replace Ourselves
videos.description:
Prized gives AI agents their own computers. Co-founder Hudson explains Hux, their 24/7 company agent that shipped a feature now driving 5% of signups, drafted 300 posts this month, and burned $17,000 in Opus credits in a week.

00:00 - Why build a company agent
01:36 - Giving it as much context as you have
03:19 - The approval loop, and teaching it your decisions
04:14 - Capping PRs so it stops just writing code
05:03 - Copying Anthropic's "superfans" for log monitoring

videos.name: Y Combinator
videos.title: How CrustData Gave Their 42nd Employee the Same Context as the Founders
videos.description:
CrustData built an internal harness called Yardmaster that sits at the core of hiring, sales, contract redlining, and P0 alerts. It took one contract from 193 redlines to zero in four rounds, and generated $674,000 in pipeline from dormant accounts in a month.

Chapters:
00:00 - What Yardmaster is, and the three things that make it work
02:05 - Hiring: transferring one person's strategy to the whole team
03:06 - Sales: ramping a new AE in a week instead of a month
04:05 - Contracts: 193 changes down to zero
05:03 - Before and after

videos.name: Y Combinator
videos.title: The On-Call Agent We Trust With Production
videos.description:
SigNoz ingests petabytes a month across a complex pipeline, and alerts used to take hours to root-cause. Co-founder and CEO Pranay shows the on-call agent that now resolves them in 90 seconds and has saved the team over 570 hours.

Chapters:
00:00 - Why on-call is hard at this scale
01:04 - An eight-hour incident, before and after
03:03 - How it works: classify, runbooks, gather, respond
04:52 - Lessons: move logic out of code, and monitor your agent like production

videos.name: Latent Space
videos.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
videos.description:
Almost half the agent work on Clay now happens in tools like Claude Code, not their own agent.

Swyx and I sat down with Jeff Barg (Head of AI at Clay) to talk about what that means for a SaaS company. Clay went from agents filling out spreadsheet cells to a coding agent that builds entire GTM workflows, which raises the question: if customers are happy driving Clay from Claude Code, why build your own agent at all? His answer is that they want to meet their customers where they are.

A few things surprised us during this conversation. Clay's lead-qualification evals have been saturated for about a year, so frontier models now only matter higher up the stack. Jeff ran the math on scoring all 40M companies in their dataset for customer fit, and it comes out to about $1,500 total. They don’t want their own agent to be markedly better than Clay + Claude Code, and usage is already close to 50/50 between Clay's agent and outside harnesses. And OpenAI pulled their ChatGPT Apps launch two days out, after they put 25% of the engineering team on it for a month, then changed their minds a few days later.

We also got into when post-training actually makes sense (Jeff's bar: $10-100M in inference spend), why Clay's agent infra is hand-rolled on BullMQ, and why agents still can't debug their own traces.

Clay: https://www.clay.com

videos.title: The Revolution vs The Renaissance — Thariq Shihipar, OpenAI
videos.description:
At AI Engineer CODE, Thariq Shihipar revisits what he got wrong about coding agents, then asks what AI makes possible when people stay in the creative loop. He shows how the /human folder lets him tune a rock attack in his fighting game and explains why he stopped using the custom Mac Dock he built. We also get into decision models and who chooses which experiments get the compute.

Recorded at AI Engineer CODE. Thariq announced that he had joined OpenAI after the interview.
